title: PSMC: Provable and Scalable Algorithms for Motif Conductance Based Graph Clustering

problem.claim: Higher-order graph clustering partitions graphs using frequently occurring subgraphs as clustering units, but existing motif-conductance methods face scalability and provable-quality limitations.

gap.claim: Existing methods rely on motif-instance enumeration and edge-weighted graph processing, with limited guarantees for some motifs and prohibitive costs on large motifs, dense graphs, and massive graphs.

contributions.claim: PSMC is a motif-conductance clustering algorithm with a fixed, motif-independent approximation ratio for any motif.
PSMC defines a locally computable Motif Resident metric, iteratively deletes the vertex with the smallest metric using dynamic updates, and returns the best result found during the process.
PSMC uses bounds to estimate vertex Motif Resident values and reduce computational costs.

author_reported_evidence.claim: On real-life and synthetic data, the authors report 3.2–32 times speedup over state-of-the-art baselines.
On real-life and synthetic data, the authors report at least 12 times higher quality than state-of-the-art baselines.

narrative_sequence.summary: Higher-order motif-based clustering is presented as a state-of-the-art approach, and motif conductance is identified as an interpretable model.
Existing motif-conductance methods depend on motif enumeration and edge-weighted graph processing, causing weak or unresolved guarantees and high computational costs.
PSMC addresses these limitations with a motif-independent approximation ratio, a locally computable vertex metric, dynamic vertex deletion, and locally optimal output selection.
Additional bounds estimate Motif Resident values to reduce computation.
The authors report substantial speedup and quality improvements on real-life and synthetic data.

source_observation.claim: The proposed method replaces global motif-instance enumeration and expensive graph processing with local metrics, dynamic updates, and estimation bounds.

interpretation.claim: When higher-order structure creates combinatorial cost, locality and incremental maintenance can be central design strategies for scalability.

application.claim: For large higher-order clustering problems, consider locally computable surrogate metrics, dynamic updates, and bounded estimation before materializing all higher-order instances.

exception.claim: The abstract does not establish whether these strategies retain the reported guarantees or performance outside the evaluated real-life and synthetic settings.

unknowns: The abstract does not specify the fixed approximation-ratio value or its proof conditions.
The abstract does not define Motif Resident or the dynamic update and estimation-bound procedures in detail.
The abstract does not provide dataset identities, experimental settings, runtime baselines, or quality metrics.
The abstract does not state limitations, resource requirements, or applicability conditions for the reported results.
